label: copy-phase input i (fed-back copy of i), from the 4th output onward
explanation: Fires only in the copy phase, when the input token is the letter i, meaning the model just output i and it is fed back in. Essentially all activation mass (>99.9%) is on in_tok == i; it never fires in the original phase, on the delimiter, or on any other input token. Within copy-phase i inputs it is gated by position: it is silent at recall_idx 0-1, weak and sparse at recall_idx 2, and fires on about 1/3 of all copy steps with i input from recall_idx 3 onward. The strongest activations come late in the copy of long sequences. Most misses are weak activations in short sequences (L = 3-4) where i is the second original token and is copied near the end. Most false positives are i inputs at recall_idx 3 in long sequences, with many outputs still to go. So magnitude rises with copy position, and possibly as the end of the sequence gets closer. It is not modulated by the output token, the previous tokens, or the first token.

issues: The core claims hold. On dev, all activation mass is in the copy phase, it is zero in the original and delimiter phases, and about 100% of mass is on in_tok == i. Output, previous and first tokens show flat lifts.

The explanation says the feature 'fires on about 1/3 of all copy steps with i input from recall_idx 3 onward'. That is false. At recall_idx >= 4 the precision is 1.000 (dev), so it fires on every copy-phase i input there. The 1/3 figure looks like the in_tok == i rate across all phases (0.276).

The real gate for recall_idx 2-3 is to_go, not position alone. At recall_idx 3, precision by to_go 0/1/2/3/4/5 is 1.00 / 0.995 / 0.81 / 0.44 / 0.34 / 0.47. At recall_idx 2 it is 1.00 / 0.92 for to_go 0/1 and about 0 for to_go >= 2. So the misses (short L = 3-4 sequences near the end) and the false positives (recall_idx 3 with many outputs left) are one systematic class: early i inputs fire only when the end of the copy is near.

The explanation says the to_go alternative lowers F1. That only holds for the version tried, '(recall_idx >= 3) | (to_go <= 2)', which pulls in recall_idx 2 with to_go 2 (precision 0.01). With to_go <= 1 instead, '(recall_idx >= 3) | (to_go <= 1)' scores test F1 0.947 (P 0.901, R 0.998, mass recall 0.9999), beating the original 0.927.

A refined predicate does better still: (recall_idx >= 4) | (to_go <= 1) | (recall_idx == 3 & to_go <= 2). Test: P 0.978, R 0.934, F1 0.955, mass recall 0.989. The original predicate scores test F1 0.927, so a clear systematic gap remains in it.
